specPoints.text: know the order of reactivity of these metals: potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, copper, silver, gold

primer.text: From Metals Reacting with Water & Acids and Metal Displacement Reactions you have built the ranking tools: vigour with water and acids, and which displacements succeed. This note fixes the full order of reactivity in memory, including where carbon and hydrogen sit among the metals, and gives a mnemonic that makes the list stick.

lessons.title: The reactivity series
sourceHeadings: Carbon and the reactivity series mnemonic
lessons.opening: The reactivity series of record runs from potassium at the top, through sodium, lithium, then calcium, magnesium and aluminium, before zinc, iron and the noble trio copper, silver, gold at the bottom. Carbon matters too: it holds a place of its own on the series, between aluminium and zinc. Hydrogen also holds a position, between iron and copper, which is why only metals above it react with dilute acids.
keyPoints: The order of record is potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, then zinc, iron, copper, silver and gold.
Carbon sits between aluminium and zinc on the reactivity series.
Hydrogen sits between iron and copper on the reactivity series.
Carbon's position matters because it is used in the extraction of metals from their oxides.
The most reactive metals sit at the top and the least reactive at the bottom.

low.restatement: Learn the ladder from potassium down to gold, and remember two extra rungs: carbon between aluminium and zinc, and hydrogen between iron and copper. The top rungs react wildly, the bottom ones barely at all.
low.analogy: Picture a leaderboard where the top names play every match furiously and the bottom names barely turn up; carbon and hydrogen hold their own fixed seats in the middle.
low.examPointer: Reproduce the full order on demand; the eleven-metal list is the exact knowledge the specification names.

medium.restatement: The series orders the eleven metals of record by descending reactivity, from potassium through aluminium and zinc to copper, silver and gold. Carbon's seat between aluminium and zinc explains its working role in pulling metals from their oxides, and hydrogen's seat between iron and copper explains the acid rule that only metals above it react.
medium.analogy: Treat the series as a seating plan at a dinner table: every element has one fixed chair, and knowing who sits where settles every question about who outranks whom.
medium.examPointer: When a question gives a partial series, place the missing element by memory of the full ladder rather than by guesswork.

check.stem: Which metal tops the reactivity series of record?

options.explanation: Potassium leads the list, ahead of sodium and lithium, which is why it reacts violently with water.
Sodium is second; potassium sits above it in the order of record.
Gold is at the bottom of the list, the least reactive metal of the eleven.
Carbon holds a middle seat between aluminium and zinc; it does not top the metal list.

check.stem: Where does carbon sit in the reactivity series?

options.explanation: Carbon's seat between aluminium and zinc is what lets it pull some metal oxides apart and not others.
Nothing sits between those two; carbon is far lower, in the middle of the ladder.

options.text: Below gold at the very bottom
options.explanation: Carbon outranks several metals including zinc and iron; it is not the bottom entry.

options.text: Carbon does not appear in the reactivity series
options.explanation: Carbon is an important element with its own place on the series, exactly as the note states.

check.stem: Hydrogen's seat is between iron and copper. Which consequence follows?

options.text: Iron reacts with dilute acids but copper does not
options.explanation: Only metals above hydrogen react with dilute acids, and iron sits above the hydrogen seat while copper sits below it.

options.text: Both iron and copper react with dilute acids
options.explanation: Copper's seat below hydrogen blocks the acid reaction; only iron qualifies.

options.text: Neither iron nor copper reacts with dilute acids
options.explanation: Iron is above hydrogen and does react; iron sulfate is a standard product.

options.text: Hydrogen displaces copper from its salts
options.explanation: Hydrogen sits below some metals and above others; displacing copper would need hydrogen to outrank it, which it does not.

check.stem: Which sequence lists three consecutive metals correctly in descending reactivity?

options.explanation: Magnesium sits above aluminium, which sits above zinc, so this rung-to-rung run is correct.
That run runs uphill; zinc sits below both magnesium and aluminium.
The true descending order there is zinc, iron, copper; this list reverses it.
Silver sits near the bottom and potassium at the top; they are not consecutive.

check.stem: Why is carbon's position described as important?

options.text: Because it is used in the extraction of metals from their oxides
options.explanation: Carbon can take oxygen from the oxides of metals below it, which is the basis of its extraction role.

options.text: Because it reacts violently with cold water
options.explanation: Carbon is not a metal and takes no part in the water reactions that rank the top of the series.

options.text: Because it makes the series longer
options.explanation: Length is beside the point; the seat matters for what carbon can and cannot reduce.

options.text: Because it is the only non-metal ever placed on the series
options.explanation: Hydrogen, also a non-metal, holds a seat too; carbon's importance comes from its extraction role.

check.stem: List the metals of the reactivity series of record in order, from the most reactive to the least reactive.
check.modelAnswer: Potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, copper, silver and gold, running from the most reactive at the top to the least reactive at the bottom.

check.stem: Where do the non-metals carbon and hydrogen sit in the reactivity series?
check.modelAnswer: Carbon sits between aluminium and zinc, and hydrogen sits between iron and copper.

check.stem: Explain why carbon's position in the reactivity series matters industrially.
check.modelAnswer: Carbon's place between aluminium and zinc decides which metal oxides it can strip oxygen from: it is used to extract metals that sit below it in the series from their oxides.

check.stem: Iron fizzes in dilute acid but copper is untouched by the same acid. Use hydrogen's seat in the series to explain the difference.
check.modelAnswer: Hydrogen sits between iron and copper, so iron lies above hydrogen and can push hydrogen out of the acid, while copper lies below hydrogen and cannot displace it, which is why copper shows no reaction.

lessons.title: The reactivity series mnemonic
lessons.opening: A mnemonic turns the eleven-metal ladder into one memorable sentence, pairing each rung with a word in order. Each word's first letter fixes a rung of the series, including carbon at cute and hydrogen at hot between the metals. The same table shows the series at work in the extraction of metals from their oxides.
keyPoints: The mnemonic reads: please send lions, then cats, next monkeys, so cute zebras, go into hot countries, all signed Gordon.
Each word's first letter gives one rung: potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, carbon, zinc, iron, hydrogen, copper, silver, gold.
Carbon appears as the word cute, between aluminium and zinc.
Hydrogen appears as the word hot, between iron and copper.
Silver and gold finish the sentence, matching their places at the bottom of the series.

low.restatement: Say the sentence once, then read off the initials: P, S, L, C, M, A, C, Z, I, H, C, S, G. Those letters are the series itself, with cute as carbon and hot as hydrogen tucked between the metals, exactly where their seats belong.
low.analogy: Like a shopping list memorised as a silly sentence: the stranger the sentence, the better it sticks when the exam asks for the list.
low.examPointer: Write the mnemonic initials down first in an exam, then expand each letter to its element; it prevents missed rungs and keeps carbon and hydrogen seats honest.

medium.restatement: The mnemonic encodes the full ladder, metals and the two non-metals alike: please, send, lions, cats, monkeys, and, cute, zebras, into, hot, countries, signed, Gordon maps to potassium through gold in order. Carbon at cute and hydrogen at hot keep their seats visible, which is what lets the mnemonic serve both the acid rule and the extraction working.
medium.analogy: Treat the sentence as a zip file for the series: thirteen small words unpack into the entire ordered list, ready whenever a question needs a rung.
medium.examPointer: Practise expanding initials to elements under time pressure, and double-check the two non-metal seats when using the list for predictions.

check.stem: Which word in the mnemonic stands for carbon?

options.explanation: Cute supplies the C that marks carbon's seat between aluminium and zinc.
Cats is the first C, and it stands for calcium, not carbon.
Countries is the third C, marking copper near the bottom of the list.
Zebras marks zinc, which sits just below carbon in the series.

check.stem: Which word marks hydrogen's seat in the mnemonic?

options.explanation: Hot gives the H for hydrogen, sitting between iron (into) and copper (countries).
Into marks iron, which sits just above hydrogen in the series.
Send marks sodium at the top of the list, nowhere near hydrogen's seat.
options.misconception: top rung confused with the middle

options.explanation: Signed marks silver, second from the bottom of the ladder.

check.stem: Which metal does the word monkeys stand for?

options.explanation: Monkeys follows cats (calcium) in the sentence, matching magnesium's rung below calcium.
Manganese is not on the eleven-metal list of record; the M is magnesium.
Mercury is not part of this series; the M rung is magnesium.
Aluminium is the next word, and, which follows monkeys in the sentence.

check.stem: A student expands the initials as P, S, L, C, M, A, C, Z, I, H, C, S, G. Which two rungs do the repeated letters remind them to place carefully?

options.text: Carbon among the C words and hydrogen at H, with the C words in the order calcium, carbon, copper
options.explanation: The three Cs and the single H are exactly where misplacements happen, and the sentence order fixes them.

options.text: Sodium and silver, because both start with S
options.explanation: The two S words sit far apart at opposite ends, so they are the easy Cs' problem, not the S words'.

options.text: Zinc and iron, because their words are longest
options.explanation: Word length is irrelevant; the initials are what map to the series.

options.text: The mnemonic has no repeated initials
options.explanation: C appears three times (cats, cute, countries), which is precisely why the repeated letters need care.

check.stem: How does the mnemonic table connect the series to extracting metals from their oxides?

options.text: Carbon, at its seat between aluminium and zinc, can pull oxygen from the oxides of metals below it
options.explanation: The seat below some metals and above others is what decides which oxides carbon can reduce.

options.text: Gold, at the bottom, is the easiest metal to extract with carbon
options.explanation: Gold's low position means it needs little help, but carbon's usefulness comes from outranking the oxide's metal.

options.text: The mnemonic itself performs the extraction
options.explanation: The sentence is a memory tool; the chemistry comes from carbon's position, not from the words.

options.text: Extraction works only for metals above carbon
options.explanation: That inverts the logic; carbon reduces the oxides of metals that sit below it.

check.stem: Which metals do the words lions, cats and monkeys stand for in the mnemonic?
check.modelAnswer: Lions stands for lithium, cats for calcium and monkeys for magnesium.

check.stem: Which two non-metals appear in the mnemonic, and which words mark their rungs?
check.modelAnswer: Carbon appears as the word cute and hydrogen appears as the word hot.

check.stem: Explain how the mnemonic keeps silver and gold in their correct places in the series.
check.modelAnswer: Silver and gold finish the sentence, matching their places at the bottom of the series as the least reactive metals, so the end of the sentence mirrors the end of the series.

check.stem: A student expands the mnemonic's rungs as P, S, L, C, M, A, C, Z, I, H, C, S, G and notices two letters repeat. Name the metals at the repeated rungs and the metals each could be confused with.
check.modelAnswer: C repeats: the first C is cute, which is carbon between aluminium and zinc, and the later C is copper. S repeats: the first S is send, which is sodium, while the final S is silver near the bottom.

glossary.definition: The full ordered ladder of elements by reactivity, including the metals of record plus carbon and hydrogen.
A memory sentence whose word initials reproduce an ordered list, here the reactivity series.
The removal of a metal from its oxide ore, which carbon's series position makes possible for some metals.
The compound of an element with oxygen, from which metals are extracted by carbon where the series allows.
The ranking of the eleven metals of record from potassium down to gold.

workedExample.prompt: a) Write the reactivity series of record for the eleven named metals. b) State where carbon and hydrogen sit on the series. c) Using carbon's position, explain why carbon can extract zinc from zinc oxide but cannot extract aluminium from aluminium oxide.
steps: a) Potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, copper, silver, gold — most reactive at the top, least reactive at the bottom.
b) Carbon sits between aluminium and zinc, and hydrogen sits between iron and copper.

c) Carbon can only remove oxygen from a metal that lies below it in the series: zinc lies below carbon, so carbon displaces zinc from its oxide, but aluminium lies above carbon, so carbon cannot extract it.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) K, Na, Li, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Cu, Ag, Au. b) Carbon between Al and Zn; hydrogen between Fe and Cu. c) Zinc is below carbon (extractable); aluminium is above it (not extractable).
